project_scope.note: Texas madrone is now the canonical clickable Ericaceae anchor. Sparkleberry remains a reference/breadth comparison pending separate strict county review.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: On local woody taxa, start with alternate exstipulate leaves and fused flowers, then inspect the anthers for apical pores.
family_diagnostics.flower: Corolla commonly fused and urn-, bell-, or tube-shaped; stamens commonly 5–10.
family_diagnostics.anthers: Poricidal anthers and anther appendages are high-value characters.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Capsule, berry, or drupe depending on lineage.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Poricidal anthers are a stronger family clue than bark or berry color.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole plant → high-value structure → reproductive confirmation → tie-breaker
visual_lesson.intro: Texas madrone and sparkleberry make a great pair because they look different as plants but share the same Ericaceae reproductive language.

steps.title: 1 · Start with Texas madrone habit
steps.image_credit: Public Domain · Gary M. Stolz / USFWS
steps.look_for: Woody evergreen/semi-evergreen architecture and distinctive smooth exfoliating trunk.
steps.why_it_matters: Gives a memorable local family anchor without using bark as the sole ID.

steps.title: 2 · Add madrone fruit
steps.image_credit: Public Domain · Gary M. Stolz / USFWS
steps.why_it_matters: Shows one Ericaceae fruit form while reminding you fruit type varies.

steps.title: 3 · Compare sparkleberry
steps.look_for: A very different woody Vaccinium form with the same fused-flower family framework.
steps.why_it_matters: Prevents overfitting Ericaceae to madrone bark or one growth form.

steps.title: 4 · Zoom to the anther pores
steps.look_for: Pollen exits through small pores at the tips of the anthers rather than long slits.
steps.why_it_matters: Poricidal anthers are one of the best technical Ericaceae confirmations.

comparisons.title: Ericaceae vs Rosaceae
comparisons.rule: Rosaceae commonly has free petals plus a hypanthium; Ericaceae commonly has a fused corolla and poricidal anthers.

comparisons.title: Ericaceae vs Ebenaceae
comparisons.rule: Both can be woody with fused flowers and fleshy fruit; Ericaceae anther architecture is the stronger tie-breaker.

visual_lesson.caveat: Ovary position and fruit type vary across Ericaceae, so neither should be memorized as one fixed family rule.
